extracted.intended_audience: DHS/regulatory analysts, policy makers, state/local governments, and immigration/stakeholder commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Methodology and regulatory compliance guidance used in DHS's Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) for the public‑charge final rule, covering how to estimate disenrollment/chilling effects, transfer payment impacts, data choices, and applicability of statutes and executive orders. Includes analytic assumptions, bounds, and non‑quantified indirect effects to be considered in rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating disenrollment/forgone enrollment rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate a rate of disenrollment or forgone enrollment in public benefits programs attributable to the rule (the 'chilling effect'). DHS used a low estimate (3.1%), an upper-bound estimate based on Bernstein et al. (2019; 2020) (14.7%), and a midpoint primary estimate (8.9%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose estimates based on relevant prior methodologies and studies; explain rationale for selecting particular studies (e.g., population match). Acknowledge that estimates may over- or under-estimate effects and that published studies vary (4.1%–48% reported reductions). Provide a range (low, primary/mid, high) due to uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation of reduction in transfer payments
rubrics_metrics.description: Total annual reduction in transfer payments is estimated by multiplying the disenrollment/forgone enrollment rate by: (1) the population of analysis (those who may disenroll/forgo enrollment in covered programs) and (2) the value of the forgone benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit each multiplicative step and inputs; present results for low, primary, and high disenrollment rates. Document data sources for population and benefit values used in multiplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population-of-analysis estimation (household/person conversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Method to estimate public benefits recipients who are members of households that include noncitizens: (a) divide number of people receiving benefits by U.S. Census average household size (2.63) to get households; (b) multiply households by 6.9% (noncitizen share of population) to estimate households with at least one noncitizen; (c) multiply those households by the foreign‑born average household size (3.31) to estimate number of noncitizen recipients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State and justify assumptions (e.g., applying 6.9% noncitizen population share across programs). Acknowledge uncertainty introduced by these steps and potential bias (over/underestimation) if noncitizens cluster in households differently than the population average.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-year selection for baseline estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a 5‑year average of public benefits recipients' data from FY2014 to FY2018 for baseline estimates; do not use FY2019–FY2021 because those years were affected by the 2019 Final Rule and the COVID‑19 pandemic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain and document why certain years are excluded (policy shocks, pandemic distortions). Prefer multi‑year averages to smooth annual variation when appropriate, and state sensitivity checks if alternate year ranges are plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating average annual benefit per person
rubrics_metrics.description: For each benefit (except Medicaid), calculate benefit per person by dividing average annual program payments by average annual total number of recipients. For Medicaid, use CMS' median per capita expenditure estimate across all States for 2018.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the best available administrative or CMS data; disclose years used and whether averages are multi‑year. For programs with state supplements (e.g., SSI) or programmatic differences across states, note limitations and where state variation cannot be quantified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal/State share assumptions for Medicaid (FMAP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the average Federal Medical Assistance Percentage (FMAP) across all States and U.S. territories (59%) to estimate the Federal share of Medicaid transfer payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that using a national average can under- or overestimate Federal shares for particular states; disclose that enhanced FMAPs and temporary FMAP changes (e.g., Families First Coronavirus Relief Act) may not be reflected and may bias estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal share assumptions for SNAP, TANF, and Federal Rental Assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Conservatively assume the Federal Government pays 100% of the benefit values included in the analysis for SNAP, TANF, and Federal Rental Assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State that this is conservative; if state/local shares exist, note inability to quantify due to data limits and potential impacts on total transfer estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of transfer payments in cost‑benefit analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Transfer payments (reductions in transfer payments) are considered transfers and therefore are not treated as costs or benefits of the rule because they are monetary payments from one group to another that do not affect total resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly separate transfers from net costs/benefits to society in the RIA; discuss distributional effects and note that transfers may nonetheless have important equity and welfare implications even if not counted as net benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study selection and justification for chilling‑effect estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Select empirical studies whose populations closely match the population of interest (e.g., Bernstein et al. target nonelderly adults foreign born or living with a foreign‑born relative), and explain exclusions (some studies focus only on low‑income subsets or omit certain programs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why one study set is used as proxy when no single study covers all programs; discuss limitations (e.g., omission of TANF/SSI from Bernstein studies) and direction of potential bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting ranges and using midpoints under uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is substantive uncertainty (e.g., rates of disenrollment ranging widely across studies), present a lower bound, upper bound, and a primary (midpoint) estimate (DHS uses midpoint 8.9% between 3.1% and 14.7%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide transparent rationale for selecting bounds and midpoint; where possible, provide sensitivity tables and discuss how conclusions change across the range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of indirect and downstream effects beyond transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Include potential additional indirect effects of disenrollment (worse health outcomes such as obesity/malnutrition and reduced prescription adherence; increased emergency room use; increased prevalence of communicable disease; increases in uncompensated care; increased poverty and housing instability; reduced productivity and educational attainment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when such effects are hard to monetize, identify and qualitatively describe them in the RIA; relate them to values in E.O. 12866/13563 (equity, human dignity, fairness) and discuss potential distributional impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: State administrative costs and 'churn' from disenrollment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess additional administrative costs incurred by States from increased churn (people cycling on/off benefits) and costs for outreach/education (e.g., grants to community organizations, staff training, call center staffing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document reported state experiences and, where available, specific dollar examples; consider both short‑term (training/grants) and ongoing operational costs (caseworker time, call centers) when estimating state burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) applicability test
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the rule directly regulates 'small entities' (small businesses, small governmental jurisdictions, small organizations). Individuals are not defined as 'small entities' under the RFA. If the rule does not directly regulate small entities, certify no significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the RFA determination and provide evidence supporting the certification (show the rule targets individuals and not small entities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA) applicability test and threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the rule contains a 'Federal mandate' that would directly result in $100 million or more (1995 dollars, inflation‑adjusted — ~ $177.8 million in 2021) in any one year for State/local/Tribal governments or the private sector. If the rule does not impose such an enforceable duty, UMRA Title II does not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define 'Federal intergovernmental mandate' and 'Federal private sector mandate' per UMRA; document why downstream voluntary effects do not count as UMRA mandates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act (SBREFA) / 'major rule' timing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If OMB designates the final rule a 'major rule' under 5 U.S.C. 804 (likely annual effect on economy >= $100M or other major impacts), the rule generally must be effective no earlier than 60 days after Congress receives DHS's report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the designation, statutory timing requirement, and effective date to demonstrate compliance with SBREFA notification/delay provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 13132 (Federalism) test
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the rule would have substantial direct effects on the States, the relationship between the Federal Government and the States, or the distribution of power and responsibilities among levels of government. If not, no federalism summary impact statement is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document analysis and conclusion about federalism implications and whether the rule preempts State law or imposes substantial direct compliance costs on State/local governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 12988 (Civil Justice Reform) drafting standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft rules to provide a clear legal standard for affected conduct and carefully review to eliminate drafting errors and ambiguities to minimize litigation and undue burden on the Federal court system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe steps taken to review and clarify statutory and regulatory language; document legal review and revisions made to reduce ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 13175 (Tribal consultation) assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the rule has 'tribal implications' — substantial direct effects on Indian Tribes or the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes. If there are no such effects, no further tribal consultation analysis is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State whether tribal implications exist and, if so, what consultation or coordination steps were taken; if none, document the basis for that determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family Policymaking Assessment (Sec. 654) criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must assess whether a regulatory action may affect family well‑being. The assessment considers seven factors: (1) impacts on family stability/safety (marital commitment); (2) impacts on parental authority in education/nurture/supervision; (3) helps family perform functions; (4) affects disposable income or poverty of families/children; (5) financial impacts justified; (6) whether impact may be carried out by State/local government or family; (7) policy on youth behavior and societal norms. If affirmative, prepare an impact assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly run through each of the seven statutory factors and document the determination. If the conclusion is that the rule does not affect family well‑being, state that and why (as DHS did).

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA applicability and use of categorical exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze whether the National Environmental Policy Act applies to the proposed action and, if so, the degree of analysis required. CEQ regulations permit agencies to establish categorical exclusions (actions that do not individually or cumulatively have a significant effect on the human environment). DHS Directive/Instruction Manual list DHS categorical exclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe NEPA screening, reference relevant DHS Directive/Instruction Manual and CEQ regulations (40 CFR 1500–1508), and state whether the action fits within an established categorical exclusion or requires an EA/EIS.

rubrics_metrics.name: SSI benefit valuation method and state supplements
rubrics_metrics.description: For SSI, use the maximum Federal benefit level effective January 1, 2022 ($841 monthly for an individual; $1,261 monthly for a couple) as the Federal baseline. Acknowledge some States supplement Federal SSI, making total benefits higher in those States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document federal maximums used, note heterogeneity due to state supplements, and explain inability to quantify state supplements if data lacking.
